keyPoints: Chapter 19
Modeling Optional and Variant Data
Modern C++ lecture with code, output, and presenter script
slides.narration: Welcome to Book II, Chapter 19: Modeling Optional and Variant Data. This deck follows the Chapter 1 Slides model: concept on the left, code or evidence on the right, and presenter notes that tell the instructor what to say and do. Modern C++ is not about using the newest syntax because it looks impressive. It is about encoding ownership, lifetime, invariants, generic behavior, and failure boundaries so the program is easier to reason about and harder to misuse.

slides.narration: The learning target is professional explanation. Learners should be able to say what Modeling Optional and Variant Data changes about program design, not merely identify a keyword. Push for three layers: the intent, the mechanism, and the evidence. In modern C++, the evidence might be a destructor running, a copy becoming independent, a move leaving ownership in exactly one place, a constrained template rejecting a bad call, or an algorithm producing a predictable sequence.

slides.narration: In Book II, Chapter 19, treat 19.2.1 Using std::variant as a design decision with costs and evidence. The parse result holds either a Reading containing an integer or an Error containing explanatory text. Callers can inspect the active alternative with holds_alternative, use checked get, or use get_if for a pointer-based query. Selecting the wrong alternative with get reports an error rather than reinterpreting arbitrary storage as the requested type. Some variant operations can produce a valueless-by-exception state under their specified conditions, so generic infrastructure should not assume every conceivable variant operation is infallible. The simple construction and visitation paths here avoid pretending to cover every throwing-alternative case. slides.narration: In Book II, Chapter 19, treat 19.3.1 Using Tuples as a design decision with costs and evidence. The example creates a tuple containing count, sum, and name. Its element types are deduced from the supplied values. Access by position is possible, but repeated get<0> and get<1> calls can obscure meaning in larger code. A tuple does not validate that count and sum correspond to the same dataset. As with an aggregate, consistency belongs to the construction logic or a stronger domain type. For a reusable reporting API, a named Summary structure may be easier to evolve and document than a positional tuple. A tuple combines heterogeneous values by position. It works well for a small local result whose structure is immediately understood, such as a total and a label produced together. It becomes less readable when callers must remember that position zero is an ID, position one is a priority, and position two is a count across distant modules. At that point a named structure often communicates the domain more effectively. slides.narration: In Book II, Chapter 19, treat Preserve information from parsing to presentation as a design decision with costs and evidence. The parser first demonstrates a compact optional result: an integer exists only when the complete input is accepted. It then demonstrates a richer variant result that retains an error message alongside successful reading values. These are two intentionally different interfaces to a similar parsing problem, not two layers that must always be stacked together. Whole-input consumption matters. Parsing an initial number from 42tail does not meet a grammar that requires one complete integer. The code checks both the error indicator and the end pointer returned by from_chars. It treats valid zero as a successful value rather than as a missing-result sentinel. Those checks preserve distinctions that the result type alone cannot enforce. slides.narration: In Book II, Chapter 19, treat Failure clinic — A default that erased an error as a design decision with costs and evidence. A reporting function replaces a rejected parse with zero and then emits a normal reading. The program no longer crashes, but the customer cannot distinguish malformed input from a genuine zero measurement. The defect is semantic information loss. The correction is not a different default number; it is preserving absence or a structured error until the policy-owning layer decides what to do. Another defect constructs a variant with the wrong first alternative and assumes that default construction means empty. A third visitor catches all unknown types in a generic success branch, allowing a newly added error alternative to be formatted as ordinary data. Test the state model directly: valid zero, another valid value, malformed syntax, out-of-range value, and every declared alternative. A graduate-level explanation should say what the abstraction buys, what rule keeps it honest, and what artifact proves the rule: source code, compiler acceptance or rejection, stdout, stderr, exit status, object state, or a test witness.
